title: Rebalancing
description: Master fixed partition counts, dynamic splitting, proportional partitioning, zero-downtime rebalancing, and handling split-brain during rebalance.

segments.text: Your cluster needs more nodes. Or a node just died. Either way, data needs to move. Rebalancing is the process of redistributing partitions across nodes, and if you get it wrong, you'll take your entire system down while trying to make it better. I've seen it happen twice, both on a Friday evening.

The fixed partition count strategy is the simplest. Decide upfront: you'll have 256 partitions. With four nodes, each gets 64 partitions. Add a fifth node, and each existing node donates some partitions to the new one. Cassandra uses 256 virtual nodes by default. The partitions don't change, only their assignment to nodes.

The trade-off with fixed partitions: you must choose the count at creation time. Too few, and individual partitions become too large to move efficiently. Too many, and the metadata overhead per partition adds up. Cassandra's recommendation: aim for 100 MB to 200 MB per partition. For a 10 TB dataset, that's roughly fifty thousand to a hundred thousand partitions.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens if your data grows 100x beyond what you planned? Can you change the partition count?

segments.text: Dynamic splitting avoids the fixed-count problem. When a partition exceeds a size threshold, it splits into two. When it shrinks, partitions merge. HBase regions work this way. A region grows to 10 GB, the RegionServer splits it and assigns the new half to another server. The system adapts to data growth automatically.

Proportional partitioning combines both ideas. The number of partitions is proportional to the number of nodes. When you add a node, new partitions are created by splitting existing ones. Cassandra's newer approach: each node gets a fixed number of partitions regardless of data size. As the cluster grows, partitions multiply proportionally.

Zero-downtime rebalancing is non-negotiable in production. The process: first, copy data from source to destination partition while still serving from the source. Second, once caught up, atomically switch reads to the new location. Third, clean up the old copy. During copying, new writes must go to both locations. This is essentially a live migration.

Rebalancing is expensive. Moving a 100 GB partition over a 10 Gbps network takes about 80 seconds. During that time, you're consuming network bandwidth that your production traffic also needs. Throttling is essential. Cassandra's streaming throughput is configurable, defaulting to 200 Mbps to avoid saturating the network. Plan rebalances during low-traffic windows.

The nightmare scenario: split-brain during rebalance. Node A thinks it owns partition P, Node B also thinks it owns partition P. Both accept writes. Now you have divergent data. This happens when the coordination mechanism, like ZooKeeper, loses connectivity during the rebalance. Fencing tokens and epoch numbers prevent this by ensuring only the latest owner's writes succeed.
segments.thought_prompt: If both nodes accept writes during split-brain, how do you reconcile the data afterward?

segments.text: Modern systems automate rebalancing carefully. Kubernetes StatefulSets handle pod replacement but not data rebalancing. CockroachDB automatically rebalances ranges when nodes join or leave, targeting uniform range counts. DynamoDB does it transparently; you never even see it happening. The best rebalancing is the kind your team doesn't have to think about.

Rebalancing is the operational tax of partitioned systems. Fixed partitions give you simplicity but require planning. Dynamic splitting adapts but adds complexity. Whatever you choose, practice it. Run rebalancing in staging before production. The worst time to learn your rebalancing process is during an incident at three AM.
